tribe: Bahra' of Quda'a — adopted into Banu Zuhra of Quraysh
teaser: The only horseman at Badr. When the Prophet ﷺ asked, he answered: we will fight at your right and your left.
quran_mention: «انفِرُوا خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا» — 'Go forth, light or heavy' — Quran 9:41, the verse he used to refuse being excused

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: A man carried under two different names
layers.content:
His name was al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr, of Bahra', a branch of Quda'a from the south. His kunya was Abu Ma'bad. Yet almost nobody in Makka called him ibn 'Amr. In the Jahiliyya he had become the ally of al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth of the Banu Zuhra, and al-Aswad adopted him. From that day he was al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad — a son by arrangement, not by blood, borrowing a lineage because he had none of his own inside the city.

Then the Qur'an ended the practice: «ادْعُوهُمْ لِآبَائِهِمْ» — 'Call them after their fathers' (33:5). Adopted men were given their own fathers' names again, and the people went back to saying al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr. He never quite lost the older name. The sources still carry both, side by side, as though neither one could be given up.

His daughter Karima described him to those who asked. He was tall and dark-skinned, thick through the middle, with a great deal of hair on his head and eyebrows that met above his eyes. He dyed his beard yellow. She remembered that he used red dye.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 33:5 — «ادْعُوهُمْ لِآبَائِهِمْ» 'Call them after their fathers'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — lineage, kunya, and the description narrated from Karima bint al-Miqdad

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: He gave up a borrowed name and a borrowed roof
layers.content:
Adoption in Makka was not sentiment. It was protection. It meant a clan would answer for you if you were harmed. Islam cost al-Miqdad exactly that.

Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi place him among those who emigrated to Abyssinia in the second emigration. Musa ibn 'Uqba and Abu Ma'shar do not mention him at all — the reports differ, and Ibn Sa'd records the disagreement rather than smoothing it over. What is not disputed is where he ended up. When he left Makka for Madina he owned no house there. He lodged with Kulthum ibn al-Hidm, together with Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, and stayed in that house until Kulthum died shortly before the army marched to Badr. Then he moved in with Sa'd ibn 'Ubada. The Prophet ﷺ tied him in brotherhood to Jabbar ibn Sakhr of the Ansar.

Later, a man of Quraysh refused to let al-Miqdad marry his daughter. The lineage was not good enough. The Prophet ﷺ answered that refusal himself: 'But I will let you marry Duba'a bint az-Zubayr ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib' — his own cousin, of the house of Hashim.
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ to al-Miqdad: 'But I will let you marry Duba'a bint az-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib' — narrated by 'Affan ibn Muslim from Hammad ibn Salama from Thabit, in Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: The one horseman on the field at Badr
layers.content:
Before Badr the Prophet ﷺ put the question to the men: this was a fight outside Madina, and no one had promised him that. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh rose for the Ansar. Then al-Miqdad rose.

'Messenger of Allah, go where Allah instructs you. We are with you. We will not say what the people of Musa said: «فَاذْهَبْ أَنتَ وَرَبُّكَ فَقَاتِلَا» — So you and your Lord go and fight (5:24). Rather we will fight at your right and your left, before you and behind you. By Allah, if you were to take us to Bark al-Ghimad, we would fight alongside you until you gained it.' The Prophet ﷺ rose at that, and the reports say it delighted him.

He brought a horse to that battle. Her name was Sabha. 'Ali said afterwards: 'There was no horseman on the Day of Badr other than al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr.' Al-Qasim ibn 'Abd ar-Rahman said: 'The first to attack on his horse in the Cause of Allah was al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad.' He was at Badr, Uhud, the Ditch and every battle after them, counted among the archers. At the conquest of Makka he held the right flank while az-Zubayr held the left.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 5:24 — the words of the people of Musa that al-Miqdad refused to repeat
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — al-Miqdad's words before Badr; 'Ali's testimony narrated through Shu'ba from Abu Ishaq; the flanks at the conquest narrated from Abu Kabsha al-Anmari

layers.title: The Trial and Quality
layers.subtitle: The hardest thing he faced was being let off
layers.content:
Al-Miqdad did not stay poor. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted him produce at Khaybar, and his family sold twelve wasqs of barley from it to Mu'awiya ibn Abu Sufyan for a hundred thousand dirhams. He was also given land among the Banu Hudayla in Madina; Ubayy ibn Ka'b called him over to that ground. The man who had arrived owning nothing ended his life a wealthy one.

Wealth and age gave him an exit, and someone offered it to him. Abu Rashid al-Hibrani said: 'I left the mosque and there was al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad at one of the money-changers' boxes, and I said to him, Allah has excused you.' Meaning: you are old, you are heavy, you have done enough, stay home.

He did not accept the excuse. He answered with the ayah: «انفِرُوا خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا» — 'Go forth, light or heavy' (9:41). The verse leaves no category of person out, and he refused to invent one for himself. The first horseman of Islam would not be retired by his own comfort.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 9:41 — «انفِرُوا خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا وَجَاهِدُوا بِأَمْوَالِكُمْ وَأَنفُسِكُمْ» 'Go forth, light or heavy, and strive with your wealth and your lives'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the Khaybar barley narrated from Musa ibn Ya'qub; the exchange narrated from Abu Rashid al-Hibrani

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: Carried three miles on the shoulders of men
layers.content:
He died in 33 AH, aged about seventy. The reports say he drank castor-oil and died of it — an ordinary death, in a bed, for a man remembered on a horse.

He died at al-Jurf, three miles outside Madina. His daughter Karima said they carried him on the shoulders of men the whole way in, so that he could be buried in Madina at al-Baqi'. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan prayed over him, and afterwards began to praise him openly. Az-Zubayr answered with two lines of verse: 'I will not find you after death makes me mourn, when you have provided me with my provision in life.'

What the ummah kept was not the horse and not the hundred thousand dirhams. It was a sentence. Every time Muslims read the account of Badr they meet a man with no clan of his own standing up to say: we will not tell you to go and fight alone. We will be at your right and your left, in front of you and behind you.

He had nothing to offer but himself, and offered it first.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — death narrated from Karima bint al-Miqdad; az-Zubayr's verse narrated from Rawh ibn 'Ubada from Shu'ba from al-Hakam

quiz.prompt: Why was he called al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad when his father's name was 'Amr?

options.text: Al-Aswad was his grandfather
Al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth had adopted him in the Jahiliyya
It was a title given to him after Badr
He took the name of the man who freed him

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Then Quran 33:5 came — 'Call them after their fathers' — and the borrowed lineage was dissolved. He was al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr again. A man's worth was moved off his ancestry and onto his own record.

quiz.prompt: Whose words did al-Miqdad refuse to repeat when he spoke before the Battle of Badr?

options.text: The words of the hypocrites of Madina
The words of Abu Jahl
The words of the people of Musa: 'So you and your Lord go and fight'
The words of the people of Nuh

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III; the ayah is Quran 5:24
quiz.scholar_reflection: He named the failure he refused to commit before he made his promise. It is easier to keep a commitment when you have already said out loud what breaking it would look like.

quiz.prompt: What did 'Ali say about al-Miqdad and the Day of Badr?

options.text: That he was the first to be wounded
That there was no horseman that day other than al-Miqdad
That he carried the banner of the Muhajirun
That he was the youngest man in the army

quiz.citation: Reported through Shu'ba from Abu Ishaq — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Muslims had seventy camels and two horses at Badr. His mare was called Sabha. One man on horseback against a hundred cavalry is not a military fact. It is a statement about what he was willing to be.

quiz.prompt: When Abu Rashid al-Hibrani told al-Miqdad 'Allah has excused you' from going out to fight, how did he answer?

options.text: He accepted and stayed in Madina
He said his sons would go in his place
He quoted the command to go forth 'light or heavy'
He said he had already given his wealth instead

quiz.citation: Narrated from Abu Rashid al-Hibrani — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; the ayah is Quran 9:41
quiz.scholar_reflection: The verse names two kinds of people, light and heavy, and commands both. He read it as leaving him no exemption to claim. He was standing at a money-changer's box when he said it — a wealthy old man arguing himself back into the field.

quiz.prompt: How was al-Miqdad's body brought into Madina for burial?

options.text: On his own horse, Sabha
Carried three miles on the shoulders of men
He was buried where he died, at al-Jurf
On a camel sent by 'Uthman

quiz.citation: Narrated from Karima bint al-Miqdad — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He died at al-Jurf, three miles out. They carried him the whole way so that he could lie at al-Baqi'. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan prayed over him. The man who had once needed someone to lend him a name was carried home by hand.

quiz.prompt: Al-Miqdad had no clan of his own in Makka. He belonged by arrangement. What do you notice in yourself when you are somewhere you have not fully been given a place?

options.text: I work harder than everyone, to earn a place I was not handed
I go quiet and wait to be told whether I am welcome
I stop needing the room's permission and simply act
I attach myself closely to whoever has already accepted me

quiz.citation: Reflection on al-Miqdad's position in Makka — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: None of these is weakness. The interesting question is what happens to that instinct after you are secure. His did not disappear — it turned into being first.

quiz.prompt: He said out loud the failure he refused to commit — 'we will not say what the people of Musa said' — before he made his promise. Do you find it useful to name what you are afraid of becoming?

options.text: Yes — it is harder to drift into something you have already refused by name
No — naming it gives it more room in my head than it deserves
Only in private. Saying it out loud feels like performance
I have never tried it and I am not sure what would happen

quiz.citation: Reflection on al-Miqdad's words before Badr
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was speaking to men who could still have said the other thing. Naming the refusal in front of them made it theirs as well as his.

quiz.prompt: A man of Quraysh refused him a marriage because of his lineage. The Prophet ﷺ answered by marrying him into the house of Hashim. What does that kind of answer do that an argument cannot?

options.text: It settles the matter without needing anyone to admit they were wrong
It shows the man his worth rather than telling him
It costs the defender something, which is why it is believed
It changes what the community treats as normal, not just what it says

quiz.citation: Narrated from Thabit — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nothing in the report suggests the Prophet ﷺ rebuked the man who refused. He simply made the refusal irrelevant.

quiz.prompt: Al-Miqdad refused an exemption he was entitled to. When you are offered a legitimate way out of something demanding, what usually decides you?

options.text: Whether I am genuinely spent, or only tired of it
Whether anyone else would notice if I stepped back
Whether stepping back would quietly change who I am
I usually take it, and then argue with myself afterwards

quiz.scholar_reflection: Exemptions in the deen are a mercy and refusing them is not always the higher road. What his answer shows is a man who checked the verse before he checked his comfort.

quiz.prompt: He arrived in Madina owning nothing and died wealthy. Which of these do you think was the harder test for him?

options.text: The poverty — it left him dependent on other men's houses
The wealth — it gave him reasons to stay home that sounded righteous
Neither. The test was the same test in two costumes
The wealth, because nobody warns you about that one

quiz.citation: Reflection on al-Miqdad's life in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sources record his poverty in one line and his hundred thousand dirhams in another. They spend more words on the moment he refused to be excused.
